label: script
not_in_script: expectations: written from her opening words, that she came to get it looked at properly
no tenderness of the scalp or temples: from the script's marking scheme, not from its conversation
investigations: the script orders none, and says that emergency imaging here is a fault

scenario.reasoning: A woman of 29 with years of one-sided throbbing headaches, nausea, dislike of light and sound, and a zig-zag visual warning of twenty minutes that clears completely; clear triggers, a mother with migraine, every red flag absent and a normal examination. This is migraine with aura, and here it is right to say so with confidence. A learner is most likely to miss asking the red-flag questions that make that confidence safe.

patient.name: Ms Priya Sharma
patient.manner: Clear and matter-of-fact, describes things well, and is quietly worried.

scenario.opening_words: Hi doctor. It's my headaches. I've had them for years, but they've been more frequent lately and I thought I'd finally get it looked at properly.

facts.fact: It is usually one side, around my temple and behind the eye. Throbbing. When it is bad I cannot really work through it.
It is mostly the right side, but sometimes the left. It moves around between attacks.
About twenty minutes before the pain, I get zig-zag lines in my vision. Shimmering, like a broken bit in the corner of my sight. Then it fades and the headache comes.
The lines in my vision go away completely, within half an hour.
I feel sick with it, and light and sound make it worse. I have to close the curtains and lie down in the dark.
An attack lasts several hours, sometimes most of a day if I cannot lie down.
I get two or three a month now. It used to be once a month, if that.
Stress sets them off, and work has been mad. So does skipping lunch, a bad night's sleep, and red wine almost every time.
My mum had migraines when she was younger. She always said mine sounded the same.
It has never come on instantly, like a thunderclap. It always builds up over twenty minutes or so.
I have no fever and no stiff neck with them.
I have no lasting weakness, numbness or trouble speaking. Once it is over, I am completely back to normal.
They never wake me from sleep, and they are not worse when I cough, strain or bend forward.

scenario.ideas: My mum always said my headaches sounded the same as her migraines.
scenario.concerns: I had half-convinced myself it was something awful.
scenario.expectations: I want to get it looked at properly at last.

plan.step: Name migraine with aura and explain it
A triptan (sumatriptan) to take as soon as the aura starts, with an anti-inflammatory such as ibuprofen or paracetamol, and a medicine for sickness if needed
A headache diary for a couple of months, and work on the triggers
Consider a daily preventer if the attacks become very frequent

scenario.safety_net: A headache that is different from her usual pattern, such as an instant thunderclap, the worst ever, one with a fever and a stiff neck, or an aura that does not clear within an hour or leaves weakness behind, needs urgent assessment, at A&E if need be.

data_gathering: Ask what a typical attack is like.
Ask about a warning before the pain, and whether it clears completely.
Ask whether a headache has ever come on like a thunderclap.
Ask about fever or a stiff neck.
Ask about lasting weakness, numbness or trouble speaking.
Examine the nervous system and look at the backs of the eyes.
management: Name migraine with aura, with confidence.
Prescribe a triptan with an anti-inflammatory, to take early.
Ask for a headache diary and discuss the triggers.
Tell her which change of headache needs urgent assessment.
relating: Find out that she feared something awful, and reassure her.
Explain why a pattern that has stayed the same for years is reassuring.
Agree with her where to start on the triggers.
